articles.title: DOGE Shut Down This Agency. Now Its Employees Are Back on the Payroll With Nothing To Do.
articles.content:
A federal agency that coordinates government homelessness programs was supposedly shuttered by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in the early days of the second Trump administration.
But the staff at the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness (USICH) were never actually fired. Instead, they were placed on paid administrative leave for several months. Then they were quietly rehired, even though the council has not held a meeting since December 2024 and has been given nothing to do.
"As of May 2026, USICH had 10 full-time employees and a part-time executive director," the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported in an audit published last week. Staff at the USICH told the GAO that "since their return, they had not received direction from the Council or the executive director on homelessness policies or priorities to guide their work or help them perform USICH's statutory duties and functions."
After the USICH staff was placed on paid leave last year, the council's office in Washington, D.C., was cleaned out and its equipment was returned to the federal General Services Administration. However, a federal judge ruled last year that the Trump administration could not shut down the USICH without congressional authorization and ordered the staff to return to work. The staff returned from leave in December and purchased new equipment, the GAO reported.
Since then, the staff seems to have had little to do. "USICH officials told us all employees were teleworking as of February 17, 2026," the GAO reported. "As of September 2026, USICH staff said they had not received direction from the Council or the executive director on federal homelessness policies or priorities to guide their work and help perform USICH's statutory duties and functions."
The USICH's official government website seems to support the GAO's conclusions. The agency's newsletter has not been updated since January 2025. Its Twitter account has been silent since November 2024—particularly telling, given the Trump administration's aggressive use of social media.
Reason's calls and emails to the USICH this week went unreturned, with one exception: An email to Makese Motley, who is still listed as the council's director of legislative affairs, generated an automated response saying that Motley left that position in August and providing an alternative email address. Contacted at that address, Motley declined to comment on the GAO report, citing "the confidentiality and nature of my current job."
The Trump administration has proposed abolishing the USICH in 2027. The council's 2026 budget request to Congress sought $250,000 to "conduct an orderly closeout of USICH, which includes sufficient funding for limited closeout activities and payroll liabilities."
If the USICH is slouching toward oblivion, that would be in keeping with Congress' original intent for the agency—which was supposed to be a temporary effort when it was established in 1987, only to have its planned termination extended several times, the GAO notes.
The Trump administration's attempt to shut down the USICH in 2025 was met with outcry. "The U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness has been vital in shaping effective policy to end homelessness," Ann Oliva, CEO of the National Alliance to End Homelessness, said in a statement to NPR in April 2025.
That's a questionable claim. As City Journal noted in 2025, shortly after the Trump administration placed the council's staff on administrative leave, the USICH oversaw a large increase in homelessness during its tenure. While it was intended to reduce overlapping governmental efforts in that space, the USICH played a key role in pushing policies that have not worked—such as reducing the number of transitional housing programs, which resulted in more homeless people living on the street.
Regardless of how you feel about the USICH, the GAO report details an unsatisfying situation. Paying federal bureaucrats not to work won't save taxpayer money and won't make the government more efficient or effective.
Unfortunately, that's happened a lot. Federal employees were paid $9.5 billion not to work during 2025, in large part because of the Trump administration's efforts to shrink the federal workforce and reduce spending, the GAO reported last month.
Shutting down the USICH seems like the right thing to do, but this once again points to the problems with DOGE's approach to cutting government. Killing useless government programs requires congressional action—or, in this case, requires Congress simply not reauthorizing the USICH when it is set to expire in 2028.

articles.title: Alito's 'Practical Originalism' Doesn't Sound Very Originalist
articles.content:
U.S. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recently took to the pages of The Wall Street Journal with an article adapted from his new book, So Ordered: An Originalist's View of the Constitution, the Court and Our Country. In the piece, Alito dubbed himself a "practical originalist" and a "working judicial originalist." But as he proceeded to actually detail his legal views, they sounded much more like the results-oriented "living constitutionalism" that originalists are supposed to oppose.
Consider what Alito had to say about the landmark gun rights case McDonald v. Chicago (2010). At issue were two closely intertwined questions. First, does the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms apply against state and local governments, just like it applies against the federal government? And second, if the Court did find that the amendment applies against the states, what is the proper constitutional means for applying it?
The historical evidence in the case all pointed in the same direction: The most thoroughly and consistently originalist way of applying the Second Amendment against the states was via the Privileges or Immunities Clause of the 14th Amendment.
But Alito rejected that originalist approach then and still rejects it now. To make his current case, Alito has enlisted the aid of the late Justice Antonin Scalia, who vocally opposed the Privileges or Immunities Clause argument during the McDonald proceedings. "Why did Scalia, a former law professor, say that?" Alito wrote in the Journal. "Because accepting the Privileges or Immunities argument would have opened a can of worms. Libertarians, social conservatives, progressives, socialists and others could all make a pitch for whatever rights they favored."
Of course, any judicial decision in support of a constitutional right may open a can of worms. If the Supreme Court strikes down one state's infringement on freedom of speech (or the right to keep and bear arms, or the right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures, or any other constitutional liberty), it necessarily risks opening a can of worms, because other people in other states whose rights may have been similarly infringed would now have a handy SCOTUS precedent to cite when they file their own constitutional grievance against the allegedly offending government.
But what's wrong with that? If the Constitution demands that the government stop acting in a certain way, why should a self-professed originalist put his fears about opening a can of worms ahead of his judicial duty to follow the constitutional text where it leads?
In the McDonald case, Scalia and Alito each gave short shrift to historical evidence about the original meaning of the 14th Amendment because they worried about libertarians and others "mak[ing] a pitch for whatever rights they favored." That approach by Scalia and Alito sounds like results-oriented judging and not like any kind of principled adherence to the Constitution's original meaning.
Alito's apparent penchant for results-oriented judging is also evident in his positive invocation of the right-wing law professor Adrian Vermeule, who has argued that conservatives should abandon originalism entirely because originalism sometimes leads to libertarian results. "Libertarian assumptions central to free-speech law and free-speech ideology" must be discarded, Vermeule has argued, because they have led to the idea "that government is forbidden to judge the quality and moral worth of public speech." According to Vermeule, "libertarian conceptions of property rights and economic rights will also have to go, insofar as they bar the state from enforcing duties of community and solidarity in the use and distribution of resources."
Citing Vermeule, Alito has now argued that "practical originalists" must not be "allergic to any evaluation of results." Like Vermeule, Alito seems to think that the Constitution is only worth following faithfully when it leads to results that he happens to find worthy.
If that now counts as a kind of originalism, all I can say is that the term no longer means what it originally meant.

articles.title: The Democrats' Socialist Moment
articles.content:
Ever since Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump crashed through the gates of American politics in 2015, the professional moderates of both major political parties have twisted their ears toward the dreaded sound of oncoming hooves.
For Republicans, the stampede is an ever-present threat, awaiting irritated instruction from the Oval Office. Even in his waning final-midterm season, Trump in 2026 managed to oust in primaries two sitting United States senators, further cementing his decadelong teardown and reconstruction of the GOP.
For Democrats, the mob has been more sporadic and unpredictable, as in the bolt-out-of-the-blue 2018 New York primary defeat of House Democratic Caucus Chair Joe Crowley by the then-unknown Sanders organizer Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. AOC is one of just two sitting members of Congress to hail from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a fringe caucus that few paid much heed back then. No longer.
When DSA heartthrob Zohran Mamdani topped a desultory field for New York City mayor in November 2025, it was still possible to shrug off the over-the-top reaction—NYC politics gadfly and Sex and the City veteran Cynthia Nixon calling him a "miracle of nature," Jon Stewart comparing the son of a movie producer and academic to Jackie Robinson—as a localized virus in a deep-blue city with too much media on its hands. But Mamdani this spring took things national, successfully endorsing in House of Representatives primaries three challengers (two DSA and one former DSA), including one inexperienced, nonsense-spewing candidate who toppled the chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.
AOC's DSA caucus in the House could conceivably triple in size, with the NYC shoo-ins potentially joined by candidates from Philadelphia, Denver, and Detroit. But the real test of the socialists' mettle will come in the Senate.
Insurgent blocs within major political parties reveal themselves by showing when they're willing to lose. The Tea Party during its productive heyday of 2009–13 backed some pretty out-there primary candidates who went on to squander some winnable general elections, such as anti–sharia law crusader Sharron Angle, who face-planted in her attempt to unseat a vulnerable Sen. Harry Reid (D–Nev.). Trump, too, has enforced loyalty by jeopardizing seats, as he did earlier this year by bouncing longtime Sen. John Cornyn (R–Texas) with the abjectly corrupt Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Nothing matters more this year for Democrats—and, arguably, the national electorate—than wresting control of the closely divided Senate, which at press time was almost universally forecast as a 50–50 toss-up. Trump's final two years in office will look a lot different should the opposition party hold the whip hand on the legislative branch's oversight and investigatory functions. And yet such is the antipathy of younger Democratic voters toward the perceived crusts of the party's establishment that the DSA and DSA-adjacent cheerleaders fought viciously to elevate three very flawed candidates to contested statewide Senate elections.
The first, Maine's rough-hewn Graham Platner, generated a bewildering-to-outsiders enthusiasm with his billionaire bashing and vituperations against Israel, before eventually withdrawing under a cloud of sexual assault allegations and residual stink over a Nazi tattoo. A second, Florida's Angie Nixon, won an upset victory over Trump 1.0 resistance hero Alex Vindman by stressing Medicare for All and peace in Gaza, then immediately began distancing herself from the DSA (which she had only recently joined, and which never endorsed her). Regardless of the Democratic primary, incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is considered the strong favorite.
The real center of DSA enthusiasm—and risk—is the third candidate, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, who won a razor-thin primary and is facing a razor-thin general election that could determine the razor-thin control of the Senate. El-Sayed, who combines some of Mamdani's telegenic charisma with the masculine anger of Platner, is not technically a DSA member (hell hath no fury like the nomenclatural hair splitting of far-left blocs!), but is nonetheless the poster child for the socialistic left in the run-up to November.
What does El-Sayed want? Medicare for All, to bury data centers in a blizzard of burdens and regulations, and above all, to sever America's tether with Israel, a country he cannot bring himself to affirm should exist. "Every definition of a Jewish state ends up in some articulation of illiberal values," he told CNN this summer. "Every single one."
That latter preoccupation has given an opening in this swing state to El-Sayed's opponent, Mike Rogers, a longtime national security and surveillance hawk–turned Trump toady. Democratic control over the Senate could come down to the perceived antisemitism accompanying the lefty table stakes of decrying Israel as a genocide-committing apartheid state.
Can a mere two handfuls of congressional DSA candidates, including some who are bound to lose, justify the round-the-clock handwringing over the "sexy socialist summer"? Perhaps, yes.
Think back now toward those nervous moderates. How will they modify their behavior so as to keep the populist wolves at bay? House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D–N.Y.) is facing widespread DSA calls to step aside after saying on Meet the Press that he does not support Medicare for All (a proposal that would be ruinously expensive while criminalizing private insurance plans, among other demerits). Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, a leading party centrist, signed an executive order in August severely restricting data centers, just 14 months after welcoming them with open arms. I had the opportunity recently to ask Sen. Chris Murphy (D–Conn.) the seemingly easy question of whether it's a good idea for the government to run grocery stores (as it soon will in Mamdani's New York), and he stammered like a middle schooler who didn't do the reading.
Numerically minor as it may be, the DSA insurgency is jerking the much larger party leftward on taxing billionaires (including California's disastrous wealth tax ballot initiative this November), blocking data centers, drastically expanding the already unaffordable entitlement state, and condemning Israel. This remains true even if El-Sayed loses: If you are more likely to lose your job in a primary election than the general, then what matters more is the passion of the grassroots mob, even if that proves to be normie poison.
Hillary Clinton staved off the Sanders challenge in 2016, but then capitulated to his followers on swaths of the Democratic Party platform, particularly on the hoary economic policies the old socialist holds dear. Joe Biden fended off a maniacally woke 2020 Democratic field, and campaigned in the general as a moderate, but then ceded much of his own economic policy to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D–Mass.) while engaging in whole-of-government initiatives promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion. If the young professional talent in a major political party tilts heavily in a certain direction, then even the graybeards are going to get spun, either as a conscious attempt to fend off an intramural challenge or as mere staffing math.
There is hope yet that prolonged exposure to the Castro-loving, Hamas-apologizing, economically illiterate young fools of the DSA will curdle their electoral fortunes after 10 years (and especially the last 10 months) of growth. But as long as there are out-and-proud socialists winning elections, there's plenty of work to be done by the anti-socialists of both parties.

articles.title: Brickbat: Bumper to Bumper
articles.content:
In Texas, the Galveston County Sheriff's Office fired Deputy Carlos Ramos after a video showed him tailgating a driver without using his emergency lights or siren, and swerving to prevent other vehicles from passing. Ramos followed the driver for an extended period, although officials have not said why. The driver was eventually pulled over but received no ticket or citation, and the sheriff's office later apologized to her. Sheriff Jimmy Fullen called the deputy's behavior "inappropriate, unacceptable, and inconsistent with the department's standards." Ramos is not facing criminal or traffic charges, but the Texas Commission on Law Enforcement will review his peace officer license.

The post Brickbat: Bumper to Bumper appeared first on Reason Magazine.
